doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Young pianists and listening to everything
summary: Pianists Mance admires today, and Benny Carter's lesson to listen to everything.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I want to ask you about young keyboard artists coming up today, who do you like? Who do you think carries on the tradition and has a good feel, a good grasp on the music?

There are a lot of young artists today. There’s a lot of them. Benny Green for one, a young piano player. And there’s another one, what’s this kid’s name, a heavy set guy, I’ll think of his name in a minute. Steven Scott is another one that I like. And then there are a lot of them who don’t have big names yet. There was one I had as a student at the New School and he’s recording on Verve now. He’s also playing organ. That’s Larry Goldings. He’s another one. There are so many of them. I don’t know I listen to everybody and one thing I don’t do much is compare or rate students unless they just can’t play. But the reason I listen to everybody, I learned this from Benny Carter years ago. Benny Carter came to New York to do a soundtrack for a terrible movie, called “A Man Called Adam.” It was a Sammy Davis movie. It went nowhere. But the music was good. Benny did the score for a movie, and Mel Torme was in the movie. So anyway we were recording the soundtrack, a period of about three days I guess. And so after we finished one day’s recording, Ornette Coleman was in town at the old Five Spot. And so some of the guys, the musicians, went by there and Benny was there. And he was there listening you know. And I think he stayed a couple of sets. So one of the guys says, “Benny, what are you doing here? This isn’t your type of music.” Benny said, “Listen, I listen to everything. It doesn’t mean that I’m going to use it or that I like it. But you have to listen to everything.” He says, “You have to be aware of what’s going on.” And so I’m the same way. I listen to a lot of things. My likes are very diversified as far as people I like. Like some of the guys, I really like Archie Shepp, the player. I do. Archie says a lot. And I like all avante garde music, that’s something I do like. Because I’m basically you might say a straight ahead, bebop, blues or whatever. But I even tell the students that I say listen to everybody. Maybe there’s something there you can use. You never know. Maybe it’s something you can incorporate into what you’re doing, to enhance it more.
